strengths: Novel problem framing focusing on emergent biases from feedback loops rather than pre-existing biases—addresses critical concern for agentic AI systems
Rigorous experimental design using well-grounded psychology paradigm with appropriate controls (Appendix F confirms no pre-existing associations)
Comprehensive evaluation: 15+ models, multiple metrics (SI/BGD/GASI with formal justification), 30 runs per condition with confidence intervals, and generalization across domains
Counterintuitive key finding: larger/newer models stratify MORE, contradicting existing bias benchmarks and revealing fundamental gap between single-turn and sequential fairness
Honest treatment of interventions: thorough exploration showing most standard approaches (CoT, temperature) fail, providing valuable negative evidence
Well-executed empirical work with clear presentation, good visualizations, and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic understanding: exploration-exploitation framing is plausible but largely inferred rather than directly measured; no analysis of confidence/uncertainty or lock-in dynamics

Experimental artificiality: fictional demographics and binary success/failure feedback differ from real hiring; Appendix I shows pre-existing biases dominate when using real demographics (GASI: 0.5→0.14-0.30), limiting generalizability

Proposed interventions largely fail, especially the most effective one (diversity bonus) which paradoxically reduces success rates when actual demographic-job mappings exist (Appendix G)—undermines practical impact
Scope limitations: only contextual bandit allocation tasks tested; no exploration of problem difficulty, real-world hiring complexity, or how results scale to realistic scenarios
Presentation issues: critical results relegated to appendices (real demographics in I, intervention paradox in G); some key comparisons lack formal significance tests

Comparison concerns: human baseline from different study rather than direct evaluation; unknown how humans perform with diversity incentives; LLMs may process feedback fundamentally differently than humans

strengths: Novel and important contribution identifying emergent biases in sequential decision-making by LLMs, distinct from static training biases
Striking finding that larger models scoring well on BBQ benchmarks are more prone to stratification, challenging current evaluation paradigms

Rigorous experimental design with three complementary metrics (SI, BGD, GASI) grounded in psychology literature, comprehensive model coverage (15+ models), and proper statistical rigor (n=30 runs, 95% CIs)
GASI metric cleverly validates that observed biases emerge during task execution rather than from training data (Appendix F evidence)
Strong generalization across domains (refugee resettlement, military conscription) and robustness checks with proper ablations on success rates, feature additions, and prompting strategies
Excellent presentation quality with clear writing, informative visualizations, and reproducible implementation details provided in appendices
Honest treatment of limitations including context-dependence of interventions and discussion of challenges when real demographic-job correlations exist
weaknesses: Incomplete mechanistic understanding of why larger models stratify more—the explanation of 'more precise inferences' is superficial given this contradicts intuition and deserves deeper investigation into in-context learning, exploitation vs. exploration trade-offs, or optimization preferences

Severely limited practical applicability of proposed interventions: diversity steering works but Appendix G shows it reduces success rates when actual demographic-job correlations exist, creating a fundamental deployment barrier

Section 5 (Interventions) presents scattered results—CoT marginal/insignificant, temperature ineffective, structural interventions mixed—with only diversity steering robust but context-dependent; paper is more diagnostic than prescriptive

Insufficient exploration of why chain-of-thought fails to encourage exploration despite prior work suggesting it helps, and limited analysis of model family differences (e.g., why does Qwen 2.5-72B CoT sometimes outperform others?)
The exploration-exploitation framing motivates the work but isn't mechanistically validated—how do we confirm LLMs are truly failing to explore vs. having different optimization preferences?

Methodological constraints including reliance on artificial groups (Appendix I shows different mechanisms with real demographics, lower GASI) and unjustified hyperparameter choices (p=0.9, 40 rounds) without sensitivity analysis
Minimal ethics statement and limited practical guidance for practitioners on when/how to deploy findings or when stratification trade-offs are acceptable

strengths: Careful experimental methodology with rigorous controls and extensive ablations (Appendices G-M) systematically ruling out alternative explanations
Novel empirical finding that frontier/larger models stratify MORE than weaker models, contradicting improvements on static benchmarks—important for understanding capability-fairness tradeoffs
Comprehensive evaluation across 15+ model families with proper statistical testing (Benjamini-Hochberg correction, 30 runs per condition, confidence intervals)
Thoughtful adaptation of psychology paradigm to probe bias emergence in interactive LLM settings, well-motivated by rise of agentic AI systems
Transparent treatment of limitations: honestly documents when interventions fail, acknowledges reduced effect with real demographics (Table 11), and provides extensive supplementary analyses
Three complementary metrics (SI, BGD, GASI) measuring distinct aspects of stratification, with clear mathematical definitions and numerical validation
Clear implications for AI safety: highlights inadequacy of static bias benchmarks and need for multifaceted objectives as models become more capable optimizers
weaknesses: Critical ecological validity limitation buried in appendices: Table 11 shows GASI drops dramatically from ~0.50-0.60 to 0.14-0.30 with real demographics, suggesting much of emergent effect is task-specific; this should be prominent in main text as it substantially qualifies real-world applicability

Diversity intervention (most effective solution) reduces success rates when true demographic-job mappings exist (Appendix K), creating practical dilemma with no clear guidance on when/whether to deploy—significantly limits actionable recommendations

Mechanistic understanding insufficient: paper claims biases result from 'exploration-exploitation trade-offs' but doesn't explain WHY LLMs exhibit insufficient exploration compared to theoretically sound algorithms; connection feels post-hoc rather than mechanistically demonstrated

Limited novelty: directly adapts Bai et al. (2025a)'s psychology paradigm with straightforward metric applications and standard interventions (temperature, CoT, prompting); main contribution is empirical finding rather than methodological advance

Unclear scope and generalization: uses artificial 40-round task with artificial demographic labels; unclear if patterns persist over longer horizons or different task structures; low success probability (p=0.9) may not reflect realistic settings

Insufficient causal mechanism analysis: demonstration that outcome signals drive GASI is necessary but not sufficient for exploration-exploitation hypothesis; alternative mechanisms (pattern-matching, confirmation bias) not adequately ruled out

Intervention effectiveness and practical guidance limited: most interventions fail; best solution has tradeoffs; no clear recommendations for practitioners on which interventions to use in real systems

strengths: Novel research question addressing gap between debiasing and actual LLM deployment in agentic systems
Well-grounded in psychology literature with validated iterative hiring paradigm from Bai et al. 2025a
Comprehensive experimental scope: 16+ models, multiple prompting strategies, 30 runs per condition, multiple task variants (refugee resettlement, conscription)
Rigorous methodology: Appendix G systematically isolates outcome signals through three ablations (sampling variance, trajectory variance, outcome signal)
Counterintuitive key finding: newer/larger models show MORE stratification despite better bias benchmark performance, challenging field assumptions
Transparent treatment of limitations including acknowledgment that diversity steering reduces success when ground-truth mappings exist (Section K)
Thorough intervention testing across three classes with honest assessment of effectiveness rather than overselling solutions
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Real-world validity concerns: experiments use artificial demographics with 40 rounds/4 groups; real demographic experiment (Section M) shows much lower GASI (0.14-0.30 vs 0.45-0.61), suggesting effects smaller or more driven by pre-existing biases when social salience increases
Limited theoretical understanding: documents THAT bias emerges but not deeply WHY; lacks analysis of why larger models stratify more or investigation of internal representations

Intervention limitations undermine practical impact: diversity steering (most effective approach) creates perverse tradeoff reducing success when real differences exist; authors acknowledge uncertainty about when to deploy interventions

Imprecise use of 'emergence' terminology: GASI measures consistency across runs but doesn't definitively prove emergence vs. learning from feedback; finding better characterized as 'learning spurious correlations from noisy in-context feedback'

Human comparison methodology concerns: unclear if all experimental conditions identical with Bai et al. 2025a; Thompson sampling baseline (SI=0.61) between random and humans complicates interpretation of whether LLMs truly exceed humans
Limited analysis of model heterogeneity: substantial variation across models (Claude 4 Sonnet direct=1.79 vs Qwen 2.5-72B CoT=0.89) deserves investigation but receives limited attention
Task simplicity limitations: warmth/competence framework captures some but not all bias dimensions; 40 rounds is short; jobs have no actual feature differences
Incomplete statistical reporting: formal hypothesis tests inconsistent; some significance claims lack explicit p-values; Benjamini-Hochberg correction mentioned only in footnote
Reasoning models incompletely analyzed: DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o3 excluded from some analyses (e.g., real demographics test, prior bias test) without clear justification
